issues.legal_issue: Failure to appoint separate representatives for wards with conflicting interests does not, by itself, render a compromise decree a nullity.
material_facts: Both parties to the pending appeals were wards whose estates were under the Court of Wards.
The same Deputy Commissioner was in charge of both estates and represented each ward in the appeals.
The Court of Wards did not appoint separate representatives for the wards before settling the appeals.
issues.conclusion: The requirement to appoint representatives was directory, and its non-compliance did not make the compromise decrees nullities.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 56 of the U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, the Court of Wards was directed to appoint representatives when wards with conflicting interests were parties to a proceeding. Whether a statutory requirement is mandatory depends on legislative intent gathered from the statute as a whole; the word “shall” is not conclusive. Sections 55, 57 and 58 do not make Section 56 mandatory, and the representatives remain subject to the Court of Wards’ general control. Section 38 empowers the Court of Wards to act for a ward’s advantage, including conducting litigation. A directory provision is intended to be obeyed, but its breach does not invalidate an act otherwise duly done. The court relied on Hari Vishnu Kamath v. Syed Ahmad Ishaque.

predicates.ward_interparty_proceeding: Two or more wards were parties to the same court proceeding.
predicates.conflicting_ward_interests: The wards had interests that conflicted in the proceeding.
predicates.separate_representatives_not_appointed: The authority responsible for the wards did not appoint a separate representative for each ward.

issues.definition: When wards with conflicting interests are parties to a proceeding and separate representatives are not appointed, the decree is not invalid for that reason alone.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise between two wards is not invalid merely because the same officer represented both wards and signed for each of them.
material_facts: The Court of Wards resolved to settle the disputes between the two wards on specified terms.
The same Deputy Commissioner signed the compromise petitions once for each ward in his respective representative capacity.
Lawyers engaged for the respective estates presented the compromise petitions to the court.
The Court of Wards had statutory authority to act for the wards and to make contracts on their behalf.
issues.conclusion: The compromise was between the two wards, not a contract made by the Deputy Commissioner with himself, and the common representation did not make the compromise invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 55 of the U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, provides for a ward to sue or be sued in the name of the Collector or another appointed person; the ward remains the party. Sections 38 and 61 empower the Court of Wards to act for wards and to make contracts on their behalf, including when both transferor and transferee are wards. The court therefore treated the settlement as a contract between the wards, notwithstanding that the same officer signed for each.

predicates.inter_ward_compromise: A settlement was made to resolve a dispute between two wards.
predicates.court_wards_authorized_settlement: The authority managing the wards resolved to settle the dispute on their behalf.
predicates.same_officer_signed_for_each_ward: One officer signed the settlement documents separately in a representative capacity for each ward.

issues.definition: Where the authority managing two wards authorizes a settlement between them, the same officer’s representative signatures for both do not make the settlement invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A court need not appoint a different guardian for a person under disability when that person already has a guardian appointed by a competent authority and the court makes no order substituting another guardian.
material_facts: One ward had been declared to be of unsound mind, and the Court of Wards had assumed superintendence of her estate.
The Deputy Commissioner had been appointed her guardian under the governing statutory scheme and was in charge of her estate.
The Deputy Commissioner also represented the opposing ward in the appeals.
The court did not appoint another guardian for the ward, and the Court of Wards was a statutory body entrusted with looking after wards’ interests.
issues.conclusion: The Deputy Commissioner was entitled to act as guardian for the appeals, and the failure to appoint another guardian did not render the compromise decrees nullities.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXXII, rule 4(2), of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides that where a person under disability has a guardian declared by a competent authority, another guardian is not to be appointed unless the court considers, for reasons recorded, that this would be for the person’s welfare. Section 27 of the U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, empowered the Court of Wards to appoint a guardian for a ward of unsound mind. The Court of Wards was a statutory body whose institutional role and constitution could be trusted to protect the ward’s interests, unlike those of a private guardian.

predicates.proceeding_involving_person_under_disabi: A person under a legal disability was a party to the proceeding.
predicates.guardian_already_appointed_by_competent_: A competent authority had already appointed a guardian for that person.
predicates.no_alternative_guardian_appointed: The court did not appoint a different guardian for the proceeding.
predicates.guardian_is_statutory_official: The existing guardian held the role under a statutory scheme entrusted with protecting the person’s interests.

issues.definition: When a person under disability already has a guardian appointed by a competent authority, the absence of a different guardian does not invalidate the decree where the existing guardian acts under a statutory scheme entrusted with protecting that person’s interests.
